'''Tyrone B. Hayes''' (born July 29, 1967) is an American [[biologist]] and professor of integrative biology at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He is known for his research in frogs, concluding that the [[herbicide]] [[atrazine]] is an [[endocrine disruptor]] that demasculinizes male frogs, causing them to display female characteristics. Hayes is an advocate for the critical review and regulation of pesticides as well as other chemicals that may cause adverse health effects. He has presented hundreds of papers, discussions, and seminars on his research's conclusion that environmental contaminants have played a major role in the global amphibian decline as well as being linked to the many [[health disparities]] that occur in minority and low income populations.

Hayes' research into atrazine as an endocrine disruptor has been contested by [[Syngenta]] – the company that manufactures atrazine – and the [[Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority]].

In 2023, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="Sanders 2023">{{cite web |last=Sanders |first=Robert |title=National Academy of Sciences elects seven from UC Berkeley |website=Berkeley News |date=May 3, 2023 |url=https://news.berkeley.edu/2023/05/03/national-academy-of-sciences-elects-seven-from-uc-berkeley |access-date=August 27, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=News - NAS | url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2023-nas-election.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230502194908/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2023-nas-election.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 2, 2023 | access-date=2026-01-30 | website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Tyrone Hayes was born in 1967 in Columbia, South Carolina to Romeo and Susie Hayes. As a child he showed great interest in lizards and frogs. He was particularly interested in the way frogs morphed from tadpoles into their adult form.  He won a state science fair with research that showed that [[Dactyloidae|anole]] lizards had to be awake in order to change color.<ref name="Mother Jones 2012">{{Cite journal |last1=Slater |first1=Dashka |title=The Frog of War |journal=Mother Jones |date=January–February 2012 |url=http://motherjones.com/environment/2011/11/tyrone-hayes-atrazine-syngenta-feud-frog-endangered}}</ref>  He graduated from Dreher High School in 1985 and earned both his A.B. and M.A. in biology in 1989 from Harvard University. His dissertation focused on the genetic and environmental mechanisms determining the sex of the [[wood frog]]. He continued his studies at the University of California, Berkeley. There he received his Ph.D. in integrative biology in 1993 for his study of the role that hormone play in mediating developmental responses to environmental changes in amphibians.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |title=Biography |url=https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/tyrone-hayes-41 |website=The History Makers |access-date=September 24, 2020}}</ref>

==Career==

After graduating from [[Harvard University]], Hayes worked as a technician and freelance consultant from 1990 to 1992 for [[Tiburon, California]]-based Biosystems, Inc.<ref name="vita">{{cite web |title=Tyrone Hayes Curriculum Vita |url=http://www.atrazinelovers.com/t2d.html |publisher=Atrazine Lovers Website |access-date=August 23, 2013}}</ref> Hayes has held an academic appointment (professorship) at the University of California, Berkeley since completing his doctoral research there in 1992;<ref name="Mother Jones 2012" /> he was hired as a graduate student instructor in 1992, became an [[assistant professor]] in 1994, associate professor in 2000, and professor in 2003 in the Department of Integrative Biology, Molecular Toxicology, Group in [[Endocrinology]], Museum of [[Vertebrate]] Zoology, Energy and Resources Group, University of California, Berkeley.<ref name="vita" /> In 2021, Hayes was appointed to the position of Department Co-Chair. He advanced to the position of associate dean for [[Diversity, Equity and Inclusion]] in the [[UC Berkeley College of Letters and Science|College of Letters and Science]] at Berkeley in 2023.<ref name="Sanders 2023"/>

Hayes’ scientific research has focused on the potential of genetic adaptation and the role of hormones in the development of the amphibian. His investigations have shown that chemical agents, such as a commonly used herbicide, have the ability to negatively impact the sexual development of the amphibian, even when such toxins are present in low concentrations. Hayes has taken an interest in the hormonal regulation and development of aggressive behavior. He has also been active with the National Science Foundation Review Panel since 1995, and he has served on several other advisory boards as well.

===Atrazine research===
{{See also|LGBT chemicals conspiracy theory}}
[[File:African clawed frogs; Xenopus laevis.jpg|thumb|left| ''Xenopus laevis'', the African Clawed frog]]
In 1997, the consulting firm EcoRisk, Inc. paid Hayes to join a panel of experts conducting studies for the Swiss pharmaceutical company [[Novartis]] (later [[Syngenta]]) on the [[herbicide]] [[atrazine]].<ref name="Mother Jones 2012" /><ref name="Aviv">{{cite magazine |last=Aviv |first=Rachel |title=A Valuable Reputation: After Tyrone Hayes said that a chemical was harmful, its maker pursued him |magazine=The New Yorker |date=February 10, 2014 |url=http://www.newyorker.com/reporting/2014/02/10/140210fa_fact_aviv?currentPage=all |access-date=February 7, 2014}}</ref> When Hayes' research found unexpected toxicities for atrazine, he reported them to the panel, however the panel and company were resistant to his findings. He wanted to repeat his work to validate it but Novartis refused funding for further research; he resigned from the panel and obtained other funding to repeat the experiments.<ref name="Mother Jones 2012" /><ref name="Aviv" />

In 2002 Hayes published findings that he says replicate what he found while he was working for EcoRisk,<ref name="Mother Jones 2012" /> that developing male [[African clawed frog]]s and [[leopard frog]]s exhibited female characteristics after exposure to atrazine, first in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' (PNAS)<ref>{{cite journal  |vauthors=Hayes TB, Collins A, Lee M, etal |title=Hermaphroditic, demasculinized frogs after exposure to the herbicide atrazine at low ecologically relevant doses |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. |volume=99 |issue=8 |pages=5476–80 |date=April 2002 |pmid=11960004 |pmc=122794 |doi=10.1073/pnas.082121499 |bibcode=2002PNAS...99.5476H |doi-access=free }}</ref> and then in [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hayes T, Haston K, Tsui M, Hoang A, Haeffele C, Vonk A |title=Herbicides: feminization of male frogs in the wild |journal=Nature |volume=419 |issue=6910 |pages=895–6 |date=October 2002 |pmid=12410298 |doi=10.1038/419895a |bibcode=2002Natur.419..895H |s2cid=4364535 }}</ref><ref name="NN">{{cite journal |author=Dalton R |title=E-mails spark ethics row |journal=Nature |volume=466 |issue=7309 |pages=913 |date=August 2010 |pmid=20725013 |doi=10.1038/466913a |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2007, Hayes was a co-author on a paper that detailed atrazine inducing [[Mammary tumor|mammary]] and [[prostate cancer]] in laboratory rodents and highlighted atrazine as a potential cause of reproductive cancers in humans.<ref name="Environ. Health Perspect.">{{Cite journal |last1=Fan |first1=W. |author2=T. Yanase |author3=H. Morinaga |author4=S. Gondo |author5=T. Okabe |author6=M. Nomura |author7=T. Komatsu |author8=K.I. Morohashi |author9=T.B. Hayes |doi=10.1289/ehp.9758 |title=Atrazine-Induced Aromatase Expression is SF-1 Dependent: Implications for Endocrine Disruption in Wildlife and Reproductive Cancers in Humans |journal=Environmental Health Perspectives |volume=115 |issue=5 |pages=720–7 |year=2007 |pmid=17520059 |pmc=1867956}}</ref> In 2007, Hayes presented results of his studies to the U.S. [[National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences]] showing [[chemical castration]] in frogs; individuals of both sexes had developed bisexual reproductive organs.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ball |first=Eddy |title=Amphibian Specialist Challenges EPA and Pesticide Manufacturers |url=http://www.niehs.nih.gov/news/newsletter/2007/april/science-amphibian.cfm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110627213132/http://www.niehs.nih.gov/news/newsletter/2007/april/science-amphibian.cfm |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 27, 2011 |work=Environmental Factor NIEHS News |publisher=National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences |access-date=February 7, 2014 |date=April 2007 |quote=I could take tap water that is regulated by the U.S. EPA," Hayes noted, "and I could chemically castrate frogs.}}</ref>
In 2010, Hayes published research in PNAS<ref>{{cite journal  |vauthors=Hayes TB, Khoury V, Narayan A, etal |title=Atrazine induces complete feminization and chemical castration in male African clawed frogs (''Xenopus laevis'') |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. |volume=107 |issue=10 |pages=4612–7 |date=March 2010 |pmid=20194757 |pmc=2842049 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0909519107 |bibcode=2010PNAS..107.4612H |doi-access=free }}</ref> describing laboratory work showing how exposure to atrazine turned male tadpoles into females with impaired fertility.<ref name="Aviv" />

The U.S. [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] (EPA) and its independent [[Scientific Advisory Panel]] (SAP) examined all available studies on this topic and concluded that "atrazine does not adversely affect amphibian gonadal development based on a review of laboratory and field studies."<ref name="EPAUpdateAmphib">{{cite web |title=Atrazine Updates: Amphibians |date=April 2010 |work=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency|EPA]] |url=https://archive.epa.gov/pesticides/reregistration/web/html/atrazine_update.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171117013525/https://archive.epa.gov/pesticides/reregistration/web/html/atrazine_update.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 17, 2017}}</ref> The EPA and its SAP made recommendations concerning proper study design needed for further investigation into this issue. As required by the EPA, two experiments were conducted under Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) and inspection by the EPA and German regulatory authorities. The paper concluded "These studies demonstrate that long-term exposure of larval ''X. laevis'' to atrazine at concentrations ranging from 0.01 to 100 microg/l does not affect growth, larval development, or sexual differentiation."<ref>{{cite journal |pmid=19008211 |year=2009 |last1=Kloas |first1=W |last2=Lutz |first2=I |last3=Springer |first3=T |last4=Krueger |first4=H |last5=Wolf |first5=J |last6=Holden |first6=L |last7=Hosmer |first7=A |title=Does atrazine influence larval development and sexual differentiation in Xenopus laevis? |volume=107 |issue=2 |pages=376–84 |doi=10.1093/toxsci/kfn232 |pmc=2639758 |journal=Toxicological Sciences}}</ref> A report written in ''Environmental Science and Technology'' (May 15, 2008) cites the independent work of researchers in Japan, who were unable to replicate Hayes' work. "The scientists found no hermaphrodite frogs; no increase in aromatase as measured by aromatase mRNA induction; and no increase in vitellogenin, another marker of feminization."<ref>{{cite journal |last=Renner |first=Rebecca |title=Atrazine Effects in ''Xenopus'' Aren't Reproducible (Perspective) |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |date=May 2008 |volume=42 |issue=10 |pages=3491–3493 |doi=10.1021/es087113j |pmid=18546678 |url=http://www.thecre.com/pdf/2008-Atrazine_ACS.pdf|bibcode=2008EnST...42.3491R |doi-access=free }}</ref>
In 2010, the [[Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority]] (APVMA) responded to Hayes' 2010 published paper,<ref>{{cite journal |pmid=20194757 |year=2010 |last1=Hayes |first1=TB |last2=Khoury |first2=V |last3=Narayan |first3=A |last4=Nazir |first4=M |last5=Park |first5=A |last6=Brown |first6=T |last7=Adame |first7=L |last8=Chan |first8=E |last9=Buchholz |first9=D | last10 = Stueve | first10 = T. |last11=Gallipeau |first11=S. |title=Atrazine induces complete feminization and chemical castration in male African clawed frogs (Xenopus laevis) |volume=107 |issue=10 |pages=4612–7 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0909519107 |pmc=2842049 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America| display-authors = 8 |bibcode=2010PNAS..107.4612H|doi-access=free }}</ref> by stating that his findings "do not provide sufficient evidence to justify a reconsideration of current regulations which are based on a very extensive dataset."<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=April 5, 2011|title=Chemicals in the News: Atrazine|url=http://www.apvma.gov.au/news_media/chemicals/atrazine.php|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120217061709/http://www.apvma.gov.au/news_media/chemicals/atrazine.php|archive-date=February 17, 2012|access-date=June 9, 2020|website=[[Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority]]}}</ref>

==Advocacy==
[[File:AtrazineUSAMap.png|thumb|right| A map of pounds per square mile of atrazine application in the U.S. in 1997]]

Since publishing his research on atrazine as an endocrine disruptor, Hayes has become an advocate for banning atrazine.<ref name=LoE>{{citation |title=Hormone Disruptors Linked To Genital Changes and Sexual Preference |url=http://www.loe.org/shows/segments.html?programID=11-P13-00001&segmentID=7 |work=Living on Earth |publisher=National Public Radio |access-date=February 7, 2014 |date=January 7, 2011}}</ref>
According to Hayes, the link between atrazine and altered "[[aromatase]] and [[estrogen]] production has been demonstrated... in fish, frogs, alligators, birds, turtles, rats and human cells", and, "I believe that the preponderance of the evidence shows atrazine to be a risk to wildlife and humans. I would not want to be exposed to it, nor do I think it should be released into the environment."<ref name=LoE /><ref name="silentspring">{{Cite web |url=http://www.truthout.org/silent-spring-has-sprung57796 |title=Silent Spring Has Sprung |author=Randall Amster |work=Truthout |date=March 19, 2010 |access-date=February 7, 2014 |author-link=Randall Amster |archive-date=June 6, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100606100420/http://www.truthout.org/silent-spring-has-sprung57796 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He travels and lectures extensively to both scientific and lay audiences.<ref name="Aviv" />

He also has raised issues of [[environmental racism]], warning that "if you’re black or Hispanic, you’re more likely to live or work in areas where you’re exposed to crap".<ref name="Aviv" />  While a biologist on the [[Public Broadcasting Service]], [[National Geographic Channel|National Geographic]] program ''Strange Days,'' he expressed his concerns for human health, particularly that of minority and low-paid workers exposure to agricultural chemicals.<ref name="StrangeDays">{{cite web |title=Tyrone Hayes, PhD. |work=Strange Days, Biographies |publisher=Public Broadcasting System |year=2013 |url=https://www.pbs.org/strangedays/episodes/troubledwaters/experts/bio_hayes_tyrone.html |access-date=August 23, 2013 |quote=I am concerned about the adverse impacts of Atrazine on endangered species and on racial/ethnic minorities. Prostate and breast cancer are two of the top causes of death in Americans age 25-40, but in particular Black and Hispanic Americans are several times more likely to die from these diseases. Ethnic minorities and people of low income are also more likely to hold the "unskilled" laborer positions in agriculture and pesticide production that would put them at higher risk of exposure and are least likely to have access to the emerging science demonstrating the dangers of exposure. Thus, this environmental and public health issue is also a racial/social justice issue because minority and working class people are the primary targets of pesticide exposure.}}</ref>

Research published by Hayes and other scientists was used as evidence in a class action lawsuit against [[Syngenta]] by 15 water providers in Illinois that was settled for 105 million dollars in May 2012,<ref name="NN" /><ref>{{cite web |title=City of Greenville v. Syngenta Crop Protection, Inc., and Syngenta AG Case No. 3:10-cv-00188-JPG-PMF |url=http://www.atrazinesettlement.com/ |publisher=City of Greenville |access-date=August 23, 2013 |archive-date=May 6, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506104414/http://atrazinesettlement.com/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Staff |title=Tillery planning to file new litigation involving atrazine |url=http://madisonrecord.com/issues/332-class-action/256733-tillery-planning-to-file-new-litigation-involving-atrazine-according-to-environmental-health-news |access-date=August 23, 2013 |newspaper=Madison County Record |date=June 19, 2013}}</ref> which reimbursed more than 1,000 water systems for the costs of filtering atrazine from drinking water, although the company denies any wrongdoing.<ref name="Aviv" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Berry |first=Ian |title=Syngenta Settles Weedkiller Lawsuit |url=https://online.wsj.com/news/articles/SB10001424052702304840904577426172221346482 |access-date=9 February 2014 |newspaper=The Wall Street Journal |date=25 May 2012}}</ref>

==Conflict with atrazine manufacturer Syngenta==
{{Further|Atrazine}}

A long running conflict between Hayes and agricultural chemical manufacturer Syngenta was described as "one of the weirdest feuds in the [[history of science]],” by Dashka Slater in her 2012 profile of Hayes in Mother Jones magazine.<ref name="Mother Jones 2012" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Basken|first=Paul|date=August 14, 2013|title=Berkeley Researcher Who Questioned Herbicide's Safety Loses Lab Financing|url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/berkeley-researcher-who-questioned-herbicides-safety-loses-lab-financing/|access-date=2021-05-28|website=www.chronicle.com}}</ref>

In 2014, ''[[The New Yorker|New Yorker]]'' writer Rachel Aviv reported that Syngenta might have been [[smear campaign|orchestrating an attack]] not only on Hayes' scientific credibility, but on other scientists as well whose studies have shown atrazine to have adverse effects on the environment and/or human and animal health.<ref name="Aviv" />

Aviv reported that Syngenta had criticized Hayes' science and conduct in press releases, letters to the editor, and through a formal ethics complaint filed at University of California-Berkeley.<ref name="Aviv" /> Internal Syngenta documents from 2005 released by a class-action lawsuit in 2014 show ways that Syngenta conspired to discredit Hayes, including attempting to get journals to retract his work, and investigating his funding and private life.<ref name="Aviv" /><ref name="SWO">{{cite web |title=Court-released documents: Exhibit 19, part1 |url=http://www.sourcewatch.org/images/f/f6/Exhibit_19_Part1.pdf |work=Source Watch |publisher=Center for Media and Democracy |access-date=February 7, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Howard |first=Clare |title=Special Report: Syngenta's campaign to protect atrazine, discredit critics |url=http://www.environmentalhealthnews.org/ehs/news/2013/atrazine |access-date=August 23, 2013 |newspaper=Environmental Health News |date=June 17, 2013}}</ref>
In one of the 2005 e-mails obtained by class-action lawsuit plaintiffs, the company's communications consultants had written about plans to track Hayes' speaking engagements and prepare audiences with Syngenta's counterpoints to Hayes's message on atrazine. Syngenta subsequently stated that many of the documents unsealed in the lawsuits refer to "ideas that were never implemented."<ref name="Aviv" />

== Allegations of workplace misconduct ==
In 2010, Syngenta forwarded an ethics complaint to the University of California Berkeley, complaining that Hayes had been sending sexually explicit and harassing e-mails to Syngenta scientists, including quoting the rapper [[DMX (rapper)|DMX]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Dalton |first=Rex |date=2010-08-18 |title=E-mails spark ethics row |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=466 |issue=7309 |pages=913 |doi=10.1038/466913a |issn=0028-0836 |pmid=20725013 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Some of these emails were obtained and published by ''[[Gawker]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nolan |first=Hamilton |title=Dr. Tyrone Hayes: Biologist, Cock-Fixated Megalomaniac Email Addict |url=http://gawker.com/5620781/dr-tyrone-hayes-biologist-cock-fixated-megalomaniac-email-addict |access-date=2020-06-09 |website=Gawker |language=en}}{{Dead link|date=May 2026}}</ref> Legal counsel from the university responded that Hayes had acknowledged sending letters having "unprofessional and offensive" content, and that he had agreed not to use similar language in future communications.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ethics complaint from Syngenta |url=http://www.atrazine.com/Amphibians/Univ_of_CA-7-19-10.pdf}}{{Dead link|date=May 2026}}</ref> According to Hayes, the situation had escalated after Syngenta executive Tim Pastoor had threatened Hayes and his family.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web |last=Slater |first=Dashka |date=2012-02-06<!-- Retrieved from "article:published" meta property tag in page source --> |title=The Frog of War |url=https://www.motherjones.com/environment/2012/02/tyrone-hayes-atrazine-syngenta-feud-frog-endangered/ |access-date=2020-10-28 |website=Mother Jones |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Filmography and other work==
Hayes' work was featured in the 2008 documentary film ''[[Flow: For Love of Water]]''.<ref>{{cite news |last=Collins |first=Cyn |title=Film note: All dried up |url=http://www.tcdailyplanet.net/article/2008/07/31/film-note-all-dried.html |access-date=August 23, 2013 |newspaper=Twin Cities Daily Planet |date=July 31, 2008}}</ref> In 2010, Hayes and filmmaker Penelope Jagessar Chaffer were featured on a TED Talk together for TEDWomen, discussing chemical exposure in pregnancy, in light of Jagessar's film: ''Toxic Baby.''<ref>{{Citation |last=Chaffer |first=Tyrone Hayes + Penelope Jagessar |title=The toxic baby |date=2012-02-13 |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/tyrone_hayes_penelope_jagessar_chaffer_the_toxic_baby |access-date=2023-04-13}}</ref> He appeared in the 2012 documentary film ''Last Call at the Oasis''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tyrone Hayes |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm2861198/?ref_=tt_cl_t5 |website=www.imdb.com |access-date=2014-06-24}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Scott |first=A.O. |title=When There Really Is Not a Drop to Drink 'Last Call at the Oasis,' a Documentary About Water Supplies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/05/04/movies/last-call-at-the-oasis-a-documentary-about-water-supplies.html?_r=0 |access-date=February 7, 2014 |newspaper=New York Times |date=May 3, 2012 |quote=Tyrone Hayes, a biologist, shows us mutant frogs, their endocrine systems scrambled by pesticide-borne chemicals.}}</ref> Hayes is the subject of ''The Frog Scientist'', a biographical book for children, first published in 2009.<ref>{{cite book |author=Pamela S. Turner |title=The Frog Scientist |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fhAykNJus_IC |year=2009 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Books for Children |isbn=978-0-618-71716-3}}</ref> Hayes appeared in another TED Talk in 2018. This talk centered around Hayes' early interest in science - particularly frogs - as well as his career development, research in endocrine disruption, his ongoing feud with Synenta, and the disproportionate way environmentally harmful chemicals affect the lives of minorities and the poor.<ref>{{Citation |last=Hayes |first=Tyrone |title=Endocrine disruption, environmental justice, and the ivory tower |date=2018-03-08 |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/tyrone_hayes_endocrine_disruption_environmental_justice_and_the_ivory_tower |access-date=2023-04-13}}</ref> In 2019, Hayes was the subject of the children's book, "There's Something in the Water", published by the nonprofit STEM4Real. The book focuses on Tyrone's early life and how his observations as a young child fueled his passion for studying frogs.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bakshi |first=Leena |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y0H4wwEACAAJ |title=There's Something in the Water |date=April 2, 2019 |publisher=Bowker Identification Services |isbn=978-0999453100 |edition=1st}}</ref>

==Personal life==

Hayes lives in California with his wife, Kathy Kim. He has won several awards for his teaching and his research, including the Distinguished Teaching Award from University of California, Berkeley in 2002 and the President's Citation Award from the American Institute of Biological Science in 2004. He was also awarded the National Geographic Emerging Explorer Award and the Jennifer Altman Award in 2005.<ref name="auto"/>
